newsitem.title: GERMANY: Jewish leader urges Bonn on Holocaust compensation.
newsitem.headline: Jewish leader urges Bonn on Holocaust compensation.

text.p: Germany's Jewish leader Ignatz Bubis urged Bonn to pay full compensation to thousands of elderly Jewish Holocaust survivors in the former eastern bloc before it was too late, a newspaper reported on Tuesday.

Holocaust victims in eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union were excluded from remuneration during the Cold War. Since the collapse of Communism, they have been paid only a fraction of amounts given to western victims, lobby groups say.

Bubis' remarks to the Tagesspiegel daily newspaper, released ahead of publication on Wednesday, came days after 83 U.S. senators protested to Chancellor Helmut Kohl in an open letter against Bonn's "continued refusal" to pay up in full.

"This problem must finally be solved. If we discuss this for another two years most of those concerned will be dead," Bubis said, referring to concentration camp survivors and former Nazi slave labourers now mainly in their 70s and 80s.

Bubis, who is a highly respected figure in Germany, said the failure to pay these Holocaust survivors was particularly macabre because convicted Nazi war criminals had received special disablement pensions for war injuries.

His appeal and the letter came before a delegation of Jewish leaders was due to visit Bonn on August 19 and 20, in what delegation members have described as a last-ditch effort to persuade the German government to change its policy.

Germany's environmentalist Greens launched a bill in January aimed at ensuring that Holocaust survivors in eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union receive similar benefits to those received by their western counterparts.

They argue that, although the German government has set money aside for them, this only amounts to a maximum of 1,000 marks ($537) in one-off payments, while those living in Germany received about 500 marks a month.

Bonn says Germany had set aside 1.5 billion marks for Jewish Holocaust survivors in Poland, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus and argued that these individual hard currency payments went a long way in the poor economies of the former eastern bloc.
But campaigners complain that victims in some countries have received no payments at all.
Germany has paid about 100 billion marks in compensation since World War Two for victims of Nazism. ($ = 1.863 German Marks)
